blocks.text: An acute asthma exacerbation is an acute or subacute worsening of asthma symptoms, including breathlessness, wheezing, cough and chest tightness, associated with a reduction in expiratory airflow.
It occurs due to increased airway inflammation, bronchial smooth muscle contraction, mucosal oedema and mucus hypersecretion, resulting in reversible or partially reversible airflow obstruction.
Severe exacerbations can progress to respiratory muscle fatigue, hypercapnia, respiratory failure and death.

rows: Dust mites, pollen, mould, animal dander

blocks.text: Important: An acute asthma exacerbation is a medical emergency when severe or life-threatening features are present. Treatment should begin immediately; investigations must not delay bronchodilator therapy.
Severity is determined by clinical features, oxygenation, lung function and response to initial treatment.

blocks.text: 1. Salbutamol and non-selective beta-blockers
Drugs such as propranolol can antagonise salbutamol and worsen bronchospasm.
2. Salbutamol and loop/thiazide diuretics
Can increase the risk of hypokalaemia.
3. Salbutamol and corticosteroids
Concurrent high-dose treatment can increase the risk of hypokalaemia.
4. Aminophylline and macrolides
Clarithromycin and erythromycin can increase theophylline concentrations, raising the risk of toxicity.
5. Aminophylline and ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin can increase theophylline concentrations and precipitate toxicity.
6. Magnesium sulphate and neuromuscular blockers
Magnesium can potentiate neuromuscular blockade, which is particularly important during anaesthesia and mechanical ventilation.
7. Corticosteroids and NSAIDs
Concurrent use increases gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding risk.

content_groups.group_title: B. Serious adverse effects and toxicity management

blocks.text: 1. Salbutamol toxicity

items.text: Reduce or stop excessive beta-2 agonist administration when clinically appropriate.
Reassess whether persistent tachypnoea is due to bronchospasm or treatment-associated lactic acidosis.

blocks.text: Important examination point: Salbutamol-induced lactic acidosis can cause compensatory hyperventilation. This may be mistaken for worsening asthma, resulting in unnecessary escalation of salbutamol.
2. Magnesium toxicity

items.text: Provide supportive respiratory and cardiovascular care.
Administer IV calcium gluconate when indicated, commonly 10 mL of 10% solution (1 g), slowly under ECG monitoring.
Consider dialysis in severe toxicity with renal failure.

blocks.text: 3. Aminophylline toxicity

items.text: Severe poisoning may require activated charcoal or extracorporeal removal under toxicology guidance.

blocks.text: 4. Corticosteroid complications
Short courses are generally well tolerated, but repeated courses contribute to cumulative steroid toxicity.

blocks.text: Mechanical ventilation is required when the patient develops respiratory failure or impending cardiorespiratory arrest despite optimal medical treatment.
Intubation should be undertaken by an experienced clinician.
Why is a low respiratory rate important?

Asthma causes prolonged expiration due to airflow obstruction. If the next breath begins before adequate expiration, air trapping occurs, causing dynamic hyperinflation and potentially severe hypotension or cardiac arrest.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Discharge counselling, follow-up, common prescribing errors and high-yield examination points

blocks.title: A patient may be considered for discharge when:

items.text: Respiratory distress has resolved or become minimal.
PEF has improved, preferably to at least 60–80% of predicted or personal best, depending on the applicable guideline and overall clinical assessment.
Oxygen saturation is satisfactory on room air.
Patient can use an inhaler correctly.
No further frequent nebulised treatment is required.
There is no evidence of impending respiratory failure.
Appropriate controller treatment and follow-up have been arranged.

content_groups.group_title: F. High-yield clinical pearls and examination points

blocks.text: 1. First-line bronchodilator
Salbutamol.
2. Additional bronchodilator in severe asthma
Ipratropium bromide.
3. Main anti-inflammatory treatment
Systemic corticosteroids, commonly prednisolone.
4. Second-line IV treatment
Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 minutes in selected adults.
5. Life-threatening sign
Silent chest.
6. Important ABG finding
Normal or rising PaCO₂ in a severely distressed asthmatic patient suggests fatigue and impending ventilatory failure.
7. Important electrolyte abnormality
Hypokalaemia due to intensive beta-2 agonist treatment.
8. Important drug toxicity
Aminophylline toxicity can cause seizures and potentially fatal arrhythmias.
9. Important complication
Dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP during mechanical ventilation.
10. Antibiotics
Not routinely indicated.
11. Discharge principle
Every patient should leave with appropriate ICS-containing asthma treatment and a written action plan.
12. Important prevention principle
Avoid SABA-only long-term asthma treatment.

content_groups.group_title: G. Quick revision: acute asthma medication doses
H. Important guideline references and prescribing updates

blocks.text: 1. GINA 2026 Strategy Report: Updated recommendations for acute asthma treatment, oxygen targets, bronchodilator dosing, ICS-formoterol and prevention of recurrent exacerbations.
2. WHO 2026 Childhood Asthma Guideline: Updated paediatric acute asthma management, including ipratropium, systemic corticosteroids and second-line magnesium sulphate.
3. BTS/SIGN acute asthma guidance: Emergency treatment, oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids and escalation.

Important 2026 oxygen-guideline update: GINA 2026 recommends controlled oxygen rather than routine high-concentration oxygen. In adults and adolescents, supplemental oxygen is generally considered when SpO₂ is below 92%, with a target of 92–95%. For children aged 6–11 years, the upper target is also 95%; younger children have age-specific targets. Some BTS/SIGN-based protocols retain 94–98%. Follow the locally adopted emergency protocol and avoid both hypoxaemia and unnecessary hyperoxia.
